topics.title: Meaning and Significance of Cost of Capital
explain: Cost of capital is the minimum return expected by providers of capital as compensation for their funds.
It acts as the cut-off rate or hurdle rate for evaluating capital budgeting projects.
It assists finance managers in choosing the cheapest source of financing while balancing risk.
It is used to discount cash flows to check whether an investment will create or destroy value.
It helps management design an optimum credit policy by comparing credit granting costs against benefits.

flow.title: Using Cost of Capital as Hurdle Rate
steps: Procure capital from investors
Identify investors expected return rate
Set minimum hurdle rate
Evaluate project cash flows
Accept project if return exceeds hurdle

topics.example: If a bank lends money at 8%, a business project must earn more than 8% to generate real profit.
remember: Cost of capital is also called hurdle rate, cut-off rate, or minimum rate of return.
mistakes: Treating cost of capital as merely the actual cash paid rather than total investor expectations.

quiz.q: Which of the following is also known as the hurdle rate or cut-off rate?
quiz.why: Cost of capital serves as the benchmark hurdle or cut-off rate for accepting investment projects.

quiz.q: Cost of capital is primarily used as a benchmark for which of the following?
o: Framing debt policies and capital budgeting
quiz.why: Cost of capital provides the benchmark for capital budgeting decisions and designing corporate debt policies.

topics.title: Factors Affecting Cost of Capital
explain: Capital cost is determined by the demand and supply of loanable funds in the economy.
Investor preferences and personal savings habits influence the total pool of available capital.
The risk-return trade-off dictates that riskier business ventures must offer higher returns.
Expected inflation leads investors to demand higher returns to preserve purchasing power.
Currency exchange rate fluctuations introduce additional risk and affect costs for multinational firms.

flow.title: How Demand Affects Cost of Capital
steps: Business investment opportunities increase
Competition for available capital rises
Investors demand higher required return
Cost of capital goes up

topics.example: When inflation rises to 7%, investors require a higher interest rate on bonds so their real savings do not decline.
remember: Higher perceived investment risk always forces the required cost of capital to rise.
mistakes: Assuming that cost of capital remains static regardless of market conditions and inflation.

quiz.q: When lucrative business opportunities increase and demand for funds exceeds supply, the cost of capital generally:
quiz.why: Higher competition among businesses for funding drives the cost of capital upward.

quiz.q: Why do investors demand higher returns during inflationary periods?
o: To prevent the erosion of purchasing power
quiz.why: Investors require higher nominal returns so that their investment returns outpace inflation and maintain purchasing power.

topics.title: Cost of Long-Term Debt (Kd)
explain: Debt holders enjoy a prior charge on operating profits before taxes but have no ownership rights.
Interest paid on debt is tax-deductible under the Income Tax Act, which creates an interest tax shield.
For irredeemable debt, cost is calculated as annual post-tax interest divided by net proceeds: Kd = I(1 - t) / NP.
For redeemable debt, approximation formula is: [I(1 - t) + (RV - NP)/n] / [(RV + NP)/2].
Under the Yield to Maturity (YTM) approach, Kd is the IRR that equates net proceeds to future cash outflows.
For convertible debentures, redemption value is taken as the higher of cash value or equity conversion value.

flow.title: Redeemable Debt Cost Calculation Steps
steps: Determine coupon interest payment
Apply tax deduction factor one minus t
Calculate net proceeds after floatation cost
Identify maturity period and redemption value
Apply approximation or IRR formula

topics.example: A 10% debenture in a company with a 35% tax rate costs only 6.5% after-tax because 3.5% is saved in income tax.
remember: Tax shield formula: Interest saving = Interest paid * Tax rate.
Net proceeds (NP) = Issue price minus floatation cost.
mistakes: Forgetting to multiply annual interest by (1 - t) to account for tax deductibility.
Calculating percentage floatation cost on market price when the problem specifies it on face value.

quiz.q: Which source of capital provides an interest tax shield to the issuing company?
quiz.why: Interest on debentures is a tax-deductible expense, whereas dividends are post-tax profit appropriations.

quiz.q: A firm issues 12% irredeemable debentures at par (Rs. 100). If the tax rate is 35%, what is the cost of debt?

topics.title: Cost of Preference Share Capital (Kp)
explain: Preference shareholders receive a fixed dividend rate before any payment is made to equity holders.
Preference dividends are an appropriation of after-tax profits, so they provide no corporate tax shield.
For irredeemable preference shares, cost equals preference dividend divided by net proceeds: Kp = PD / P0.
For redeemable preference shares, approximation formula is: [PD + (RV - NP)/n] / [(RV + NP)/2].
The present value method (YTM) finds the discount rate equating net proceeds to future dividends and redemption value.

flow.title: Computing Cost of Preference Shares
steps: Calculate stated annual preference dividend
Deduct floatation cost to get net proceeds
Identify redemption value and maturity tenure
Calculate Kp without tax adjustment

topics.example: A 10% preference share of Rs. 100 issued at Rs. 95 has an irredeemable cost of Kp = 10 / 95 = 10.53%.
remember: Never adjust preference dividends for tax savings because dividends are paid out of post-tax profits.
Redeemable preference shares follow the same structure as debt, substituting PD for I(1 - t).
mistakes: Deducting income tax from preference dividends as if they were debt interest payments.

quiz.q: Payment of dividend to preference shareholders is treated as:
quiz.why: Preference dividend is distributed out of profits after tax and does not reduce company tax liability.

quiz.q: XYZ Ltd. issues 10% preference shares of Rs. 100 each at Rs. 95. What is the cost of irredeemable preference shares?

topics.title: Cost of Equity Share Capital (Ke)
explain: Cost of equity represents the return required by equity shareholders given the risks they bear.
Dividend Price Approach assumes constant future dividends: Ke = D / P0.
Earnings Price Approach links share price to expected constant earnings: Ke = E / P.
Gordon Growth Model accounts for constant dividend growth: Ke = (D1 / P0) + g, where D1 = D0(1 + g).
Realized Yield Approach estimates return based on historical realized dividend yields and price gains.
CAPM Approach calculates cost based on market risk: Ke = Rf + Beta * (Rm - Rf).

flow.title: Cost of Equity under Gordon Model
steps: Identify last dividend paid D0
Apply growth rate to find D1
Identify current market price P0
Subtract floatation cost if newly issued
Add growth rate g to dividend yield

topics.example: If a share trades at Rs. 20, pays a next dividend of Rs. 2, and grows at 5% annually, Ke = (2 / 20) + 0.05 = 15%.
remember: Gordon Model: Ke = (D1 / P0) + g where D1 is next year expected dividend.
CAPM formula: Ke = Rf + Beta * (Rm - Rf), where (Rm - Rf) is the market risk premium.
mistakes: Using D0 instead of next expected dividend D1 in Gordon's dividend growth formula.
Confusing market return (Rm) with market risk premium (Rm - Rf) in the CAPM equation.

quiz.q: Under CAPM, if Rf = 5%, Rm = 10%, and Ke = 15%, what is the value of beta?
Which assumption is NOT made by the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM)?
o: Investors lend or borrow at a risk-free rate
Investors do not have the same expectations about risk and return
Investor decisions are based on a single-time period
quiz.why: CAPM assumes all investors have identical, homogeneous expectations regarding risk and return.

topics.title: Cost of Retained Earnings (Kr)
explain: Retained earnings have an opportunity cost: the returns shareholders forgo by not receiving cash dividends.
Formulas for calculating Kr are identical to Ke (Dividend, Earning, Gordon, and CAPM approaches).
Floatation costs are never deducted when calculating Kr because retained funds require no new public issue.
Cost of equity (Ke) is generally higher than Kr due to new issue pricing discounts and floatation costs.
When market value weights are used, equity market value is split between equity and retained earnings based on their book values.

flow.title: Retained Earnings Decision Mechanism
steps: Company generates net profit after tax
Decide to retain earnings instead of dividends
Assess shareholders opportunity cost of foregone dividends
Apply Ke formula excluding floatation expenses
Obtain cost of retained earnings Kr

topics.example: A company pays Rs. 10 dividend next year on a Rs. 200 share with 5% growth; Kr is (10 / 200) + 0.05 = 10%.
remember: Never deduct floatation costs when computing the cost of retained earnings (Kr).
Retained earnings are not free capital; they carry an opportunity cost.
mistakes: Assuming retained earnings have zero cost since no explicit interest or dividend is promised.
Deducting floatation costs from market price while computing Kr.

quiz.q: The cost of retained earnings is conceptually equal to:
o: Zero, because it is internal money
The opportunity cost of dividends foregone by shareholders
quiz.why: Retained earnings represent funds belonging to shareholders, carrying an opportunity cost of foregone external returns.

quiz.q: Why is the cost of retained earnings normally lower than the cost of new equity shares?
o: Because retained earnings carry lower business risk
Because retained earnings do not incur floatation costs
Because retained earnings enjoy tax deductibility
Because retained earnings have a maturity date
quiz.why: New equity issues incur underwriting and issuance floatation costs, making Ke higher than Kr.

topics.title: Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC)
explain: WACC is the weighted average after-tax cost of all capital sources used by a firm.
Weights represent the relative proportions of debt, preference shares, equity, and retained earnings in total capital.
Book Value weights use balance sheet figures, which are stable and simple to extract.
Market Value weights reflect current financial reality and market pricing, making them theoretically superior.
Since retained earnings have no separate market quote, market equity value is apportioned in the ratio of book values.
WACC serves as the overall hurdle rate for evaluating company-wide performance and new investment options.

flow.title: Steps to Compute WACC
steps: Calculate specific cost of each source
Determine total capital using chosen weights
Calculate proportion of each capital component
Multiply specific cost by respective weight
Sum all weighted costs to find WACC

topics.example: If a firm has 70% equity at 10% cost and 30% debt at 3.5% after-tax cost, WACC = (0.70 * 10%) + (0.30 * 3.5%) = 8.05%.
remember: WACC = Sum of (Weight * Specific Cost of Capital).
To apportion market equity value: use Book Value of Equity to Book Value of Retained Earnings ratio.
mistakes: Using before-tax cost of debt instead of after-tax cost in WACC calculations.
Forgetting that total weights must sum up to 1.0 (or 100%).

quiz.q: A firm has 70% equity and 30% debt. Cost of equity is 10%, loan interest is 5%, and corporate tax is 30%. What is WACC?
When calculating WACC using market value weights, how is the market value of retained earnings determined?
o: It is taken as equal to its book value
Market value of equity is apportioned between share capital and retained earnings in their book value ratio
It is valued at the redemption price of preference shares
quiz.why: Retained earnings have no separate quotation, so equity market value is divided based on book value proportions.

topics.title: Marginal Cost of Capital
explain: Marginal cost of capital is the cost incurred in raising an additional rupee of new capital.
It is computed by applying intended new financing proportions (marginal weights) to marginal component costs.
Because marginal weights reflect future raising intentions, the dilemma between book and market weights does not arise.
If a firm raises funds in unchanged proportions and component costs remain flat, marginal cost equals WACC.
When internal retained earnings are exhausted, new equity incurs floatation costs, causing marginal cost to rise.
Similarly, borrowing beyond lenders' comfort limits increases interest rates, causing the marginal cost to rise sharply.

flow.title: Marginal Cost Analysis Process
steps: Determine total additional funds required
Identify target debt and equity mix
Check limit of available retained earnings
Determine breakpoint where component costs change
Compute weighted cost using marginal proportions

topics.example: Borrowing up to Rs. 1,80,000 costs 5% after-tax, but borrowing past that incurs 8%, driving up marginal cost of capital.
remember: Break point in capital = Total available cheaper fund / Proportion of that source.
Marginal weights represent the intended proportion of new funds to be employed.
mistakes: Using historical capital weights instead of the intended new financing proportions for marginal cost.
Continuing to use Kr instead of the higher Ke after retained earnings are completely spent.

quiz.q: Marginal cost of capital is defined as the cost of:
o: Raising an additional rupee of capital
quiz.why: Marginal cost refers to the incremental cost incurred when raising additional funds over existing capital.

quiz.q: When a firm exhausts its available retained earnings and issues new external equity, marginal cost of capital generally:
quiz.why: External equity involves floatation expenses and potential underpricing, making Ke higher than Kr and raising marginal cost.
